m1-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Create a Google Colab notebook that saves itself to your Google Drive.
  • Run a code cell, add a text cell, and use the run shortcuts on your keyboard.
  • Import scikit-learn, pandas, NumPy, and matplotlib and print their versions.
  • Fix the setup problems that stop beginners most often.

In the next lesson, a program you write will read four measurements of a flower it has never seen and tell you its species. The whole thing is five lines of Python. Those five lines need a place to run, with the right libraries installed, and that's all this lesson sets up.

You'll use Google Colab, a free notebook that runs in your browser. Google's computers do the work, so it runs the same on a school Chromebook as on a gaming PC, and the machine-learning libraries this course uses are already installed. Expect the whole setup to take about ten minutes.

#What you need

  • A computer with an up-to-date web browser. Chrome works best with Colab, but Edge, Firefox, and Safari work too.
  • A Google account. A personal Gmail account is the safest choice, because some schools switch Colab off for student accounts.
  • An internet connection while you work.

You don't need a graphics card, a paid plan, or any software installs. Every lesson in this course runs on Colab's free CPU machines in seconds.

#What happens when you press Run

A Colab notebook is a page made of cells. A code cell holds Python; a text cell holds notes. When you run a code cell, your browser sends the code to a computer in a Google data center (Colab calls it the runtime), Python runs it there, and the result comes back and appears under the cell.

Two things follow from that picture. Your notebook file is safe in Drive even if you close the tab. But the runtime's memory (every variable you made) is temporary, and it's wiped when the runtime shuts down.

#Step 1: Create your first notebook

These steps are the same on every computer.

  1. Go to colab.research.google.com and sign in with your Google account (the Sign in button is at the top right).
  2. A window called Open notebook appears. Click New notebook. If the window doesn't appear, use the menu: File → New notebook in Drive. (Typing colab.new in the address bar is a shortcut that does the same thing.)
  3. At the top left, click the name Untitled0.ipynb and change it to m1-setup.ipynb.
  4. Click inside the gray code cell, type the line below, and press Shift + Enter.

The first run takes a few seconds because Colab has to start a runtime for you. Once it's connected, the top right shows small RAM and Disk meters, a number like [1] appears beside the cell, and the text prints underneath.

You'll press these hundreds of times. The menu equivalents live under Runtime, but the keys are faster.

  • Ctrl + Enter: run the cell and stay on it.
  • Ctrl + M, then B: add a new code cell below.
  • Ctrl + M, then M: turn the current cell into a text cell.

macOS

  • Shift + Return: run the cell and move to the next one.
  • Cmd + Return: run the cell and stay on it.
  • Cmd + M, then B: add a new code cell below.
  • Cmd + M, then M: turn the current cell into a text cell.

Chromebook

  • Shift + Enter: run the cell and move to the next one.
  • Ctrl + Enter: run the cell and stay on it.
  • Ctrl + M, then B: add a new code cell below.
  • Ctrl + M, then M: turn the current cell into a text cell.

The full list is under Tools → Keyboard shortcuts. Try adding a text cell now with the + Text button and typing a line like "Module 1 setup check". Text cells are where you'll write down what you noticed, which matters more than it sounds once you have ten notebooks.

This course uses four libraries. scikit-learn has the models. pandas holds tables. NumPy does fast math on arrays of numbers. matplotlib draws charts. Paste this into a new code cell and run it:

Look at the first line. The library is called scikit-learn when people talk about it or install it, but the Python name you import is sklearn. The as pd, as np, and as plt parts give the other libraries short nicknames, and nearly every tutorial on the internet uses those same three.

#Fixes for the problems beginners actually hit

A page saying you need access, or that your organization or administrator doesn't allow this app. Your school's Google account has Colab turned off. Switch to a personal Google account with the profile picture at the top right, or ask your teacher which account to use.

SyntaxError: invalid syntax on an import line. You probably wrote the install name instead of the import name. Python reads the dash in scikit-learn as a minus sign:

Change it to import sklearn.

NameError: name 'pd' is not defined. The runtime restarted (or you opened the notebook fresh) and you ran a cell that uses pd before the cell that imports it. Variables don't survive a restart, but your code does, so run the import cell again, or use Runtime → Run all to run every cell from the top.

"Cannot connect to GPU backend" or a message about usage limits. Someone switched the notebook to a GPU. This course never needs one. Open Runtime → Change runtime type, pick CPU, and click Save.

"Runtime disconnected" after a break. Colab shuts down runtimes that sit idle for a while, and free sessions also have a maximum length. Click Reconnect, then Runtime → Run all. Your notebook is untouched; only the variables need rebuilding.

⚠️ Watch out

Don't type pip install sklearn to fix an import problem. That old package name now fails on purpose with a message telling you to use scikit-learn. In Colab you almost never need to install anything for this course, because the libraries come preinstalled.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1You open yesterday's notebook and run only the last cell, which uses pd.DataFrame. What happens?

  • The notebook file keeps your code, but variables and imports live in the runtime's memory, which was wiped.

  • A fresh runtime hasn't run import pandas as pd yet. Run the import cell first, or use Runtime → Run all.

  • pandas is installed in Colab. The problem is that this runtime hasn't imported it yet.

Show answer

B. A fresh runtime hasn't run import pandas as pd yet. Run the import cell first, or use Runtime → Run all.

2Which line correctly imports scikit-learn?

  • The dash makes this a syntax error. That spelling is only for talking about or installing the library.

  • The installed package is called scikit-learn, but its Python name is sklearn.

  • Close, but there's no module by that name, so Python raises ModuleNotFoundError.

Show answer

B. The installed package is called scikit-learn, but its Python name is sklearn.

3Where does Colab keep your notebook file?

  • New notebooks save there automatically, so you can find them from Drive or from File → Open notebook.

  • The runtime is temporary. Your notebook file is saved to Drive, separately from the runtime.

  • Colab autosaves to Drive. Ctrl + S saves right away, but you don't depend on it.

Show answer

A. New notebooks save there automatically, so you can find them from Drive or from File → Open notebook.

Key takeaways

  • Colab is a free notebook in your browser; code runs on a Google runtime and the notebook saves to your Drive.
  • Shift + Enter runs a cell and moves on; Ctrl + Enter (Cmd + Return on a Mac) runs it and stays put.
  • You install scikit-learn but import sklearn.
  • After a restart or disconnect, rerun your cells from the top: the code survives, the variables don't.

  • Colab FAQ (opens in a new tab): Google's own answers on cost, session limits, and where your code runs.
  • Installing scikit-learn (opens in a new tab): what to do if you choose the offline route and an install goes wrong.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Train a scikit-learn model and use it to name the species of a new flower.
  • Explain what each of the five lines does, in your own words.
  • Turn the model's numeric answers into species names.
  • Test the model on flowers it didn't learn from and count its mistakes.

In 1936 the statistician Ronald Fisher published a table of 150 iris flowers, measured by the botanist Edgar Anderson. There are three species, 50 flowers each, and four measurements per flower: the length and width of its sepals (the green leaf-like parts under the bloom) and of its petals, all in centimeters. The table is small enough to read in a few minutes, and it ships inside scikit-learn.

Here's the question you'll answer: given the four measurements of a flower nobody has labeled, which species is it? Open a new Colab notebook called m1-first-model.ipynb and follow along.

#Five lines, one prediction

The model looked at a flower with a 5.0 cm sepal length, 3.4 cm sepal width, 1.5 cm petal length, and 0.2 cm petal width, and answered [0]. Species number 0 is setosa, and that's right: those are textbook setosa measurements.

#What each line did

  1. load_iris is a function that hands you the flower table. Nothing is downloaded; the data is stored inside scikit-learn.
  2. KNeighborsClassifier is a kind of model called k-nearest neighbors. To classify a new flower, it finds the 5 flowers in its memory with the most similar measurements and lets them vote. You'll build one by hand in Module 4.
  3. return_X_y=True splits the table in two. X holds the measurements (150 rows, 4 columns). y holds the answers, one species number per row.
  4. KNeighborsClassifier() creates an empty model, and .fit(X, y) trains it on the examples. For this model, "training" means storing the flowers so it can search them later.
  5. .predict(...) asks for a species. The double brackets matter: the outer list is a list of flowers, and each inner list is one flower's four numbers.

That pattern of creating a model, calling fit with examples and answers, then calling predict on new examples is the same for every model in scikit-learn. Learn it once and you can use dozens of models.

#Turn numbers into species names

A species number is hard to read. The full dataset object (load it without return_X_y) carries the names too:

iris.target_names[predictions] uses the array of predictions as positions in the list of names, so 0 becomes setosa, 1 becomes versicolor, and 2 becomes virginica. One call to predict handled all three flowers at once.

#See why the model can tell them apart

Plot two of the four measurements, petal length against petal width, with a color for each species. The three new flowers are the black crosses.

Setosa sits alone at the bottom left, far from everything. Versicolor and virginica are neighbors whose edges touch. Each black cross lands inside one cluster, so its five nearest flowers agree, and the model's answers match what your eyes would say. If a flower landed on the border between versicolor and virginica, the vote could go either way. Keep that in mind for the next section.

#Peek at the table with pandas

So far X has been a bare grid of numbers. Ask for a pandas DataFrame and you can see it as a labeled table:

(In Colab, a cell whose last line is just flowers.head() shows the table with neat formatting, no print needed. The two set_option lines only make plain printed tables wide enough to show every column.) The shape (150, 5) means 150 rows (one per flower) and 5 columns: the four measurements plus the target column that holds the species number. value_counts confirms 50 flowers of each species.

#Test it on flowers it has never seen

Asking about flowers the model memorized proves nothing; that's like grading a test after showing the student the answer key. A fairer check hides some labeled flowers during training, then asks the model about them. train_test_split does the hiding. Module 3 covers it properly; for now, read it as "put 30 random flowers in a drawer."

The model trained on 120 flowers and named 28 of the 30 hidden ones correctly. Both mistakes are versicolor flowers that it called virginica, with petal lengths near 4.9 cm. Find 4.9 on the chart's horizontal axis: that's exactly where the two clusters overlap. Wrong answers on borderline examples are normal, and seeing where they happen tells you more about a model than its score does.

⚠️ Watch out

Single brackets cause the most common first error. predict expects a list of examples, even when you only have one:

The message begins Expected 2D array, got 1D array instead: scikit-learn wanted a table (rows and columns) and got a flat list. Its last line suggests reshape, but the plainer fix is brackets. Wrap the flower in a second pair of brackets, [[5.0, 3.4, 1.5, 0.2]], and it works.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1After model = KNeighborsClassifier().fit(X, y), what does model.predict([[6.5, 3.0, 5.5, 2.0]]) give back?

  • predict returns an array of species numbers, one per flower. You get the name with iris.target_names.

  • That's what the 2 means, but predict returns numbers here because y holds numbers.

  • predict returns answers, not measurements.

Show answer

A. predict returns an array of species numbers, one per flower. You get the name with iris.target_names.

2Why does predict need [[5.0, 3.4, 1.5, 0.2]] with two pairs of brackets?

  • A plain list of decimals is fine in Python. The rule comes from scikit-learn.

  • Every model predicts for many rows at once, so even one flower must be a row inside a list.

  • The model type was chosen when you created KNeighborsClassifier().

Show answer

B. Every model predicts for many rows at once, so even one flower must be a row inside a list.

3Why test on 30 hidden flowers instead of the 150 the model trained on?

  • They're randomly chosen, so they're neither easier nor harder on purpose.

  • It will predict on any rows you give it, which is exactly why you have to be careful.

  • The hidden flowers act like the new, unlabeled flowers you actually care about.

Show answer

C. The hidden flowers act like the new, unlabeled flowers you actually care about.

Key takeaways

  • X is the table of measurements (rows are examples, columns are features); y is the answer for each row.
  • Every scikit-learn model follows the same steps: create it, fit(X, y), then predict(new_rows).
  • predict takes a table, so one example still goes inside a second pair of brackets.
  • Judge a model on examples it didn't train on, and look at which examples it gets wrong.

#Further reading

  • load_iris reference (opens in a new tab): every option for loading the dataset, including as_frame.
  • Getting started with scikit-learn (opens in a new tab): a one-page tour of fitting, predicting, and the other ideas this course builds on.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Find, copy, download, and restore your notebooks from Google Drive.
  • Name and lay out a notebook so it runs from top to bottom after a restart.
  • Read a scikit-learn traceback from the last line up and find the line you wrote that caused it.
  • Look up any scikit-learn function's settings without leaving the notebook.

Yesterday your notebook printed "Right: 28 out of 30". Today you open it, click the last cell, press Shift + Enter, and get NameError: name 'X_test' is not defined. Nothing is broken. The notebook file kept your code, but yesterday's runtime, and every variable in it, is gone.

Almost every confusing notebook problem in this course comes from one of three things: not finding a file, cells that were run in a strange order, or an error message nobody read to the end. This lesson handles all three.

#Where your notebooks live

Every notebook you create in Colab saves itself to My Drive → Colab Notebooks in Google Drive. You don't have to press anything, though Ctrl + S (Cmd + S on a Mac) saves immediately if you're nervous.

Four menu items cover nearly everything else you'll need:

  • File → Open notebook lists your recent notebooks and everything in your Drive.
  • File → Save a copy in Drive makes your own editable copy. Use it whenever you open a notebook someone shared with you, so your changes go into your copy and not theirs.
  • File → Download → Download .ipynb saves the file to your computer, which is handy for a backup or for handing in work.
  • File → Revision history shows earlier saved versions, so you can get back code you deleted by accident.

💡 Tip

Make one Drive folder for this course, such as Beginner ML, and move your notebooks into it as you finish them. Moving a notebook in Drive doesn't break it; Colab opens it from wherever it is.

#Name notebooks so you can find them in Module 7

Twenty notebooks called Untitled3.ipynb are useless. Start each name with the module and lesson, then a few words about it: m1-first-model.ipynb, m2-pizza-predictor.ipynb, m3-practice-scaling.ipynb. Sorted by name, they line up in course order.

Inside, keep the same shape every time. A reader (including you, later) should be able to run it from the top and understand each part:

Putting every import in one cell near the top means a single run of that cell fixes most NameErrors after a reconnect.

#Cells remember the order you ran them

The numbers beside each cell, like [4], record the order cells actually ran. That order can differ from the order on the page, and it can include the same cell twice. Running a cell a second time is exactly like pasting its code in again. Step through this program and watch score:

The page shows one cell that adds 10, but score ends at 70. In ML notebooks the same thing happens when you rerun a cell that adds a column, drops rows, or rescales data, and the second run quietly changes the result.

The fix is a habit. Before you call a notebook finished, choose Runtime → Restart session and run all. That wipes the runtime and runs every cell once, top to bottom. If it reaches the end without errors and the numbers still make sense, the notebook is trustworthy. If it breaks, you've found a cell that depended on something you ran by hand and later deleted.

#Read a scikit-learn error from the bottom up

Here's a realistic mistake. The model learned from all four iris measurements, then someone asked it about a flower using only three numbers:

That's a lot of text, and most of it is scikit-learn's own code. Read it this way:

  1. Start at the last line. It names the error type and, in scikit-learn, usually says exactly what's wrong: the model expects 4 features and got 3.
  2. Find your own line. Scan upward for the code you wrote. Here it's the line marked main.py; in Colab, your cell's line is marked with an arrow like ---->. Lines inside sklearn/ are where the problem was noticed, not where it was caused.
  3. Print what you passed. Check the shape and type of whatever went into that line.
  4. Check the docs for the function on that line.
  5. Search the exact last line, in quotes, or ask someone. Bring the error and the few lines of code that cause it.

Step 3 settles this one in two lines:

The model learned from rows of 4 numbers, and the question was a row of 3. Every row you predict on needs the same columns, in the same order, as the rows the model trained on.

#Look things up without leaving the notebook

Every model has settings, and you can print them. get_params shows the ones you didn't choose, too:

n_neighbors: 5 is the number of neighbors that vote, which you'll change in Module 4. To read the full documentation for a function, run help(KNeighborsClassifier) in a cell. In Colab you can also type a question mark after a name and run it, which opens the docs in a help panel:

For longer explanations with pictures, the scikit-learn website has a page for every class, and its examples are written by the people who wrote the code.

#Ask for help well

When you're stuck after the five steps, ask a teacher, a classmate, or a forum, and include three things: what you're trying to do, the full error (copied, not retyped), and the smallest piece of code that still causes it. Shrinking the code often reveals the bug before anyone answers.

Colab also has a built-in AI assistant that can explain an error message. Use it to understand what went wrong, then write the fix yourself. If it writes your code for you, you'll get through the lesson without learning the part the lesson was for.

⚠️ Watch out

Don't hit Run all again and again hoping an error goes away. If the same line fails twice, the cause is in your code or your data, and rereading the last line of the error is faster than rerunning.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1A cell contains df["price"] = df["price"] * 2. You run it twice by accident. What happened to price?

  • Colab runs a cell every time you ask it to, even if it ran before.

  • Each run multiplies the current values by 2, so two runs multiply them by 4.

  • Running code never undoes earlier runs. Restart and run all to get back to a clean state.

Show answer

B. Each run multiplies the current values by 2, so two runs multiply them by 4.

2A traceback is 40 lines long. Where do you look first?

  • The first line is usually just "Traceback (most recent call last)".

  • The last line names the problem, and your own line shows where you caused it.

  • Those show where scikit-learn noticed the problem. The cause is almost always in what your code passed in.

Show answer

B. The last line names the problem, and your own line shows where you caused it.

3When is a notebook ready to hand in or come back to later?

  • Outputs can come from cells run in an order the page doesn't show.

  • Saving keeps the file, but it says nothing about whether the code runs.

  • That proves the notebook works from a blank runtime, in the order written.

Show answer

C. That proves the notebook works from a blank runtime, in the order written.

Key takeaways

  • Notebooks save to My Drive → Colab Notebooks; use Save a copy in Drive for anything shared with you.
  • Name notebooks by module and lesson, and keep imports in one cell at the top.
  • Run order, not page order, decides what a variable holds. Restart session and run all is the final test.
  • Read errors from the last line up, find your own line, then print the shapes and types you passed in.

#Further reading

  • Errors and exceptions (opens in a new tab): the official Python tutorial on how tracebacks and exceptions work.
  • scikit-learn API reference (opens in a new tab): one page per class and function, with every setting and its default.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Describe the steps of a machine-learning workflow, from a question to a prediction on new data.
  • Split a table into a feature table X and a target column y with pandas.
  • Reject columns that are identifiers or that aren't known yet when the prediction is needed.
  • Tell a classification problem from a regression problem by looking at the target.

A pizza shop wants its app to say "your order arrives in about 31 minutes" the moment a customer taps Order. The shop has a log of past orders. Here are eight of them:

Six columns. Which ones should a model learn from? Not all of them, and picking wrong is one of the most common ways a model ends up looking great in testing and failing in real use. This lesson gives you a test for every column, and the vocabulary that every ML tutorial and library assumes you know.

#The workflow, from question to prediction

Every supervised machine-learning project, from a pizza timer to a hospital's risk score, follows the same loop. "Supervised" means you have past examples with the right answers attached, like orders whose delivery time you already know.

This module is about step C, the one that's easiest to get wrong without noticing. Module 3 handles the split, and Modules 4 to 7 are about models and how to judge them.

#Rows are examples, columns are features

In a machine-learning table, each row is one example: one order, one flower, one patient. Each column you feed the model is a feature, one measurable fact about the example. The column you want to predict is the target (some books call it the label).

scikit-learn uses two names for these, and you'll see them everywhere:

  • X (capital) is the feature table: one row per example, one column per feature. It's two-dimensional.
  • y (lowercase) is the target: one value per example. It's one-dimensional.

The capital letter is a math habit (capitals for tables, lowercase for lists), and it's worth keeping because everyone else does. Here's a real dataset from scikit-learn: 442 diabetes patients, 10 measurements each, and a target that scores how much each patient's disease progressed a year later.

X has shape (442, 10): 442 rows, 10 columns. y has shape (442,), a single column with one number per patient. Those two shapes must agree on the first number, because row 17 of X and value 17 of y describe the same person. (The feature values look odd, like an age of 0.038, because scikit-learn's copy of this dataset comes with every column already rescaled.)

To see what "a feature with signal" means, plot one useful feature next to one useless one:

On the left, patients with a higher BMI tend to have higher scores, so knowing BMI helps you guess. On the right there's no pattern at all: knowing that a patient is row 300 tells you nothing about their health.

#The "would I know it yet?" test

Back to the pizza log. Go through it column by column and ask two questions. Does this column describe the order in a way that could plausibly affect the answer? And will I know its value at the moment I need the prediction, when the customer taps Order?

Column Role Why
order_id drop An identifier. Every value is unique, so there's no pattern to learn, like the row number above.
distance_km feature Known from the address when the order is placed, and longer trips take longer.
pizzas feature Known at order time, and bigger orders take longer to make.
raining feature Known at order time from a weather check.
driver_tip drop The customer tips at the door, after delivery. The app can't know it when it has to make the prediction.
minutes target This is what you want to predict.

driver_tip is the sneaky one. It's probably related to the delivery time (fast deliveries might get bigger tips, or longer trips might), so a model would happily use it, and it would score well on the old log. Then, in the real app, the tip column would be empty, and the model would have nothing to work with. Using information that won't exist at prediction time is called leakage, and it's behind a lot of models that worked in testing and failed in real use.

With the roles decided, building X and y takes two lines:

Selecting with a list of column names, like orders[feature_columns] or orders[["pizzas"]], gives you a DataFrame, which is two-dimensional. Selecting with one name and no list, like orders["minutes"], gives you a Series, which is one-dimensional. That's exactly the difference between X and y.

#What X and y look like without pandas

pandas hides the bookkeeping. Step through this version to watch each order become one row of X and one entry of y:

X ends as a list of lists (a table), y as a flat list, and both have three entries because there were three orders. The id never makes it into either.

#Classification or regression? Look at the target

What kind of model you need depends on what y holds:

  • Regression: the target is a quantity on a scale, like delivery minutes, a price, or a temperature. Being off by 2 is better than being off by 20.
  • Classification: the target is a category from a fixed set, like an iris species, "spam" or "not spam", or "late" or "on time".

The same log can be turned into either kind of problem. The question you ask decides it:

Don't decide just by checking whether the column contains numbers. Zip codes, jersey numbers, and the iris species codes 0, 1, 2 are numbers that are really category names: species 2 isn't "twice" species 1.

#Every model speaks fit and predict

scikit-learn calls every model an estimator, and every estimator works the same way. Here are two very different regression models, a straight line and a nearest-neighbors averager, trained and used with identical code:

Same fit(X, y), same predict, different answers, because each model learned something different from the same eight orders. Notice that new_order has the same three columns as X, with the same names. A model can only answer questions asked in the language it learned.

Eight orders is far too few to trust either number. In the next lesson you'll build the real version from 300 orders and measure how far off it is.

⚠️ Watch out

Mistake 1: a single feature in single brackets. orders["distance_km"] is a one-dimensional Series, and fit refuses it:

The fix is orders[["distance_km"]], a table with one column.

Mistake 2: the target hiding in X. If you build X with orders.drop(columns=["order_id"]), the minutes column is still in it. The model then predicts minutes from minutes and scores perfectly. Whenever a score looks too good, check X.columns for the answer.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A school wants to predict, at the start of term, whether a student will pass a course. Which column must you leave out of X?

  • That's known at the start of term, so it's a fair feature.

  • It doesn't exist yet at the start of term. Using it is leakage, and it would make the model look far better than it can be.

  • That's already known when the prediction is made.

Show answer

B. It doesn't exist yet at the start of term. Using it is leakage, and it would make the model look far better than it can be.

2X.shape is (500, 8). What must y.shape be?

  • y has one value per example (row), not per feature.

  • Each of the 500 rows of X needs exactly one target value.

  • y is a single column of answers, so it's one-dimensional.

Show answer

B. Each of the 500 rows of X needs exactly one target value.

3You predict the number of stars (1 to 5) a customer will give a pizza. Which is true?

  • Numbers alone don't decide it. What matters is whether you treat the target as a scale or as categories.

  • You could treat it that way, but you could also treat it as a scale where 4 is between 3 and 5.

  • Regression rewards being close; classification counts any wrong star as simply wrong.

Show answer

C. Regression rewards being close; classification counts any wrong star as simply wrong.

4Why does order_id make a bad feature?

  • Like the row number in the diabetes chart, it has no pattern to learn from.

  • scikit-learn will happily use it. That's why you have to drop it yourself.

  • It is known, but being known isn't enough; the column also has to carry information.

Show answer

A. Like the row number in the diabetes chart, it has no pattern to learn from.

Key takeaways

  • Rows are examples, columns are features, and the column you want to predict is the target.
  • X is a two-dimensional table of features; y is a one-dimensional column with one target per row.
  • Drop identifiers, and drop any column that won't be known at the moment you need the prediction.
  • A target that's a quantity means regression; a target that's a category means classification.
  • Every scikit-learn estimator uses fit(X, y) and then predict(new_X), and new_X needs the same columns as X.

What you'll learn

  • Write a column plan that records each column's role and whether it's known at prediction time.
  • Build X and y from that plan instead of by hand.
  • Measure a model's error in minutes and compare it with a baseline that always guesses the average.
  • Recognize a too-good-to-be-true score as a sign of leakage.

You're going to build the thing the pizza shop asked for in the last lesson: a function that takes a new order and answers "about how many minutes?" Here's where the build ends up, with the real output from the finished notebook:

And here's the path from the shop's order log to that function:

Open a new Colab notebook named m2-pizza-predictor.ipynb. Each step below is one cell.

#Step 1: Load the order log

A real shop would export this from its ordering system. You'll make a realistic one with NumPy's random number generator, so everyone gets identical numbers. The default_rng(7) seed is what makes your log match this page.

Each row is one order, listed oldest first. Two columns are new compared with the last lesson. kitchen_minutes comes from the oven timer: how long the order took to make. drive_minutes comes from the driver's phone: how long the trip took. Both are real, useful-looking data. Keep an eye on them.

#Step 2: Write the column plan

Before touching a model, write down what every column is for. A dictionary is enough, and it doubles as documentation for anyone who reads your notebook later:

The check at the bottom matters more than it looks. When someone adds a column to the log next month, this line will name it instead of letting it slip silently into, or out of, your model.

Both timer columns fail the "would I know it yet?" test. When the customer taps Order, the pizza hasn't been made and the driver hasn't left.

#Step 3: Build X and y from the plan

Now let the plan pick the columns, so the plan and the code can't disagree:

Four features, 300 rows, one target value per row.

#Step 4: Keep the newest orders for checking

You'll test the model on orders it never trained on. Since the log is in time order, the fairest test is the most recent orders: train on the past, check on the "future".

.iloc[:240] means "rows 0 up to, but not including, 240". In Module 3 you'll meet train_test_split, which shuffles before splitting; for a time-ordered log, cutting at a date like this is often the better choice.

#Step 5: Set a baseline, then train a model

How good is "good"? Start with the laziest possible prediction: guess the average training delivery time for every order. Any real model has to beat this.

The error measure is mean absolute error (MAE): for each test order, take the gap between the guess and the truth in minutes, ignore its sign, and average the gaps. An MAE of 5 means "off by 5 minutes on a typical order".

The model roughly halves the baseline's error. It learned that distance, pizza count, rain, and time of day all push delivery times up, and by how much. (LinearRegression multiplies each feature by a learned weight and adds them up; you'll see exactly how it picks the weights in Module 4.)

To see where it's right and wrong, plot each test order's prediction against what really happened:

Most points sit within a few minutes of the line. There's no area where the model is badly off in one direction, which is what you want to see.

#Step 6: See what the leaky columns would do

Suppose you'd skipped the plan and used every column except the id and the target. Try it:

Off by about a quarter of a minute. That isn't a better model; it's adding up the two timers, because kitchen time plus drive time is the delivery time. In the app, at the moment of ordering, both timers are blank, and this model would have nothing to go on.

Remember the feeling of this number. When a score is far better than seems possible, the first thing to check is whether X contains the answer, or something recorded after the answer was known.

#Step 7: Give the model a better feature

Here's a legitimate improvement. The model treats hour as a number, so it can only learn "later is slower" in a straight line. But kitchens are slowest during the dinner rush and then calm down again. A feature that says "is it rush hour?" describes that directly:

The error drops again, and this time it's honest: whether it's 6:30 p.m. is known the moment someone orders. Inventing useful columns from the ones you have is called feature engineering, and it often helps more than switching models. Notice that the column plan stayed the single place where the decision lives.

#Step 8: Wrap it in a function

The shop's app needs one call per order. The function builds a one-row table with exactly the columns the model trained on, in the same order:

The [features] at the end of the DataFrame(...) line reorders the columns to match training, so a typo or a different order in the dictionary can't scramble the inputs.

#The finished predictor

Here's everything in one cell, ready to paste into a fresh notebook. It reuses the orders table from Step 1.

The assert line is the column-plan check from Step 2 in its strictest form: the notebook stops with a clear message if the log ever has a column the plan doesn't mention.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the plan drop kitchen_minutes, even though it clearly relates to delivery time?

  • LinearRegression handles decimals fine.

  • A feature has to be known at prediction time. This one only exists once the cooking is done.

  • On the old log it makes the model look far more accurate. That's exactly the trap.

Show answer

B. A feature has to be known at prediction time. This one only exists once the cooking is done.

2The model's MAE was compared with "always guess the average". Why bother?

  • There's no such requirement; the baseline is your own check.

  • If the lazy guess were nearly as good, the model would add little. Halving its error shows real learning.

  • It could be used that way, but its job in this build is to give the model's score some meaning.

Show answer

B. If the lazy guess were nearly as good, the model would add little. Halving its error shows real learning.

3Why train on the first 240 orders and test on the last 60, instead of the other way round?

  • In real use the model always predicts orders that come after everything it learned from.

  • They're generated the same way as the rest, so they're no easier.

  • iloc can take any range of rows.

Show answer

A. In real use the model always predicts orders that come after everything it learned from.

Key takeaways

  • Write a column plan before training: each column's role, and why dropped columns were dropped.
  • Build X and y from the plan so your code and your reasoning can't drift apart.
  • Report error in the target's own units (minutes here), and always next to a simple baseline.
  • A near-perfect score usually means a leak. Look for columns recorded after the answer was known.
  • New features made from existing ones, like rush_hour, can beat a fancier model.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a weekend column to the log generator that makes weekend kitchens slower, put it in the plan, and see if the error drops.
  • Print model.coef_ next to features. Each number is how many extra minutes the model adds per unit of that feature. Does "minutes per pizza" look reasonable?
  • Swap LinearRegression() for KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=10) from sklearn.neighbors. Same fit, same predict. Which has the lower error on this data?

#Further reading

  • mean_absolute_error (opens in a new tab): the exact formula and its options.
  • Common pitfalls and recommended practices (opens in a new tab): scikit-learn's own guide to the mistakes that make scores look better than they are, including leakage.

#Exercise 4: Classification or regression?

For each target, decide whether it's a classification or a regression problem, and write one sentence why:

  2. Which of 26 letters a handwritten character is.

What you'll learn

  • Split data into training and test sets with train_test_split, and explain why the split comes first.
  • Use stratify to keep class proportions the same in both sets.
  • Explain why k-nearest neighbors needs scaled features, and scale them with StandardScaler.
  • Fit preprocessing on training rows only, so no test information leaks into the model.
  • Turn a text category into numbers with one-hot encoding.

Train a 1-nearest-neighbor model on the breast tissue samples from the last practice, then ask it about the very samples it trained on:

100% on the training rows. That isn't skill. Ask a 1-nearest-neighbor model about a sample it has stored, and the nearest sample is that same sample, so it copies the answer. On the rows it never saw, the score falls to about 92%, and that's the number that tells you how it will do in a clinic. score here means accuracy: the fraction of predictions that are correct.

#Why a model can't grade its own homework

A model's score on its own training rows measures memory. What you care about is generalization: how well it does on new examples. The only way to estimate that is to hide some labeled rows before training, then score the model on them once at the end. Those hidden rows are the test set; the rest are the training set.

Think of it like a practice exam. If a teacher hands out the exact questions the day before, a perfect score tells you nothing about what the students learned. The test set is the set of questions nobody has seen.

#Splitting with train_test_split

Why not just take the last 30 rows as the test set? Because datasets are often sorted. The iris table lists all 50 setosa first, then versicolor, then virginica:

A test set made of the last 30 rows would contain only virginica, and a model that had never seen enough virginica during training would be tested on nothing else. train_test_split shuffles the rows before cutting, so both parts get a fair mix:

It returns four things, always in this order: training features, test features, training targets, test targets. test_size=0.2 keeps 20% for testing (you can also give a count, like test_size=30). random_state=0 fixes the shuffle so you get the same split every run; any whole number works, and changing it gives a different, equally fair split. Notice the species counts in this test set: 11, 13, and 6. Fair, but not even, which leads to the next problem.

Here's what happens inside, on six rows. Step through it and watch the list get shuffled, then cut:

#Keep the class mix with stratify

Shuffling is fair on average, but a single shuffle can be unlucky, especially when one class is rare. Here are 100 made-up examples where only 10 belong to class 1. Watch how many of them land in a 20-row test set for six different shuffles:

Without stratifying, the test set got anywhere from 1 to 3 of the rare cases, so judging the model on them is partly luck. With stratify=y_rare, the split keeps each class's share the same in both parts, so the test set always holds exactly 10% of class 1, which is 2 of 20. For classification, pass stratify=y unless you have a reason not to.

#The test set is sacred

Hiding the test rows only works if they stay hidden from every decision, not just from fit. Three rules:

  1. Split first, before you scale, encode, choose features, or look closely at patterns.
  2. Never fit anything on the test rows. Not the model, not a scaler, not an encoder.
  3. Score on the test set at the end, not after every small change. If you keep adjusting until the test score goes up, you've slowly trained on it by hand. Later modules show how to compare options without touching it.

#Why k-NN needs features on the same scale

k-nearest neighbors decides which samples are "near" by measuring distance, and distance adds up the differences in every feature. Look at how differently spread out the 30 breast tissue features are:

Take two samples whose mean area differs by 100 and whose mean smoothness differs by 0.02. Squared and added (the way distance is computed), area contributes 10,000 and smoothness contributes 0.0004. Smoothness might be the more useful clue, but k-NN can barely see it. The model is effectively using only the handful of features with big numbers.

The fix is to put every feature on the same footing. Standardizing subtracts each feature's mean and divides by its standard deviation:

After that, every feature has mean 0 and standard deviation 1, and a value of 2 means "two standard deviations above average", whatever the original unit was. scikit-learn's StandardScaler does exactly this. Compare k-NN on raw and scaled features:

Same model, same data, same split, and the test accuracy rises from about 92% to 95% just by changing units. Models based on distance (k-NN) or on gradual steps (Module 4's gradient descent) need scaling. Decision trees, which ask one feature at a time "is it bigger than this?", don't care about units at all.

#Fit the scaler on training rows only

Look at the code again. scaler.fit(X_train) learns the mean and standard deviation from training rows only, then transform applies those same numbers to both sets. That order isn't fussiness. If the scaler learned from all rows, the test set's values would shape how training data gets scaled: a little information about the "unseen" rows would leak into training, and the test score would no longer be an honest preview.

Keeping track of fit and transform by hand gets error-prone. A pipeline chains the steps so that fit runs them in the right order on training data, and score or predict reuses what was learned:

Same score as the manual version, with no way to accidentally fit the scaler on test rows.

#Turning categories into numbers: one-hot encoding

Models need numbers, but plenty of useful columns hold words. Here's a tiny bike-share log where each trip starts at one of three stations:

Why not just number the stations 0, 1, 2? Because a model would read those as quantities: "north" would be twice "harbor", and "campus" would be closer to "harbor" than to "north". None of that means anything. One-hot encoding gives each category its own 0-or-1 column instead, so every station is equally different from every other. pd.get_dummies does it in one line, which is handy for exploring.

For a model, use scikit-learn's OneHotEncoder. It learns the categories during fit (on training rows, like the scaler) and then encodes any later data with exactly the same columns, even data with a category it never saw:

harbor becomes [0, 1, 0]. airport wasn't in the training data, so with handle_unknown="ignore" it becomes all zeros instead of crashing. sparse_output=False returns a normal array you can print; without it you get a memory-saving format that prints less readably.

⚠️ Watch out

Calling fit_transform on the test set. scaler.fit_transform(X_test) re-learns the mean and standard deviation from the test rows, so training and test data end up scaled by different rulers, and the test rows' own statistics leak in. Fit once on training data; on test data, only ever call transform.

Scaling before splitting. StandardScaler().fit_transform(X) followed by train_test_split lets the test rows shape the scaling. On a big, well-behaved dataset the score may barely change, which makes this bug easy to miss; with smaller data or other preprocessing steps the damage gets bigger. Split first, every time.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A model scores 100% on its training rows and 71% on its test rows. Which number should you report as its expected accuracy on new data?

  • Training rows measure memory, not how the model does on examples it hasn't seen.

  • That's the honest estimate. The gap between the two numbers is also a warning sign you'll study in Module 7.

  • Averaging mixes an honest number with a dishonest one, which isn't a meaningful estimate.

Show answer

B. That's the honest estimate. The gap between the two numbers is also a warning sign you'll study in Module 7.

2Which code scales the data without leaking test information?

  • The scaler learned from every row, including the future test rows.

  • The scaler's mean and standard deviation come only from training rows.

  • The second fit_transform re-learns from the test rows, so the two sets are scaled differently.

Show answer

B. The scaler's mean and standard deviation come only from training rows.

3You're classifying a rare condition that appears in 5% of rows. Why use stratify=y?

  • It keeps the proportion the same; it doesn't change it.

  • Without it, a small test set might get almost none of the rare cases.

  • train_test_split shuffles by default. stratify controls the class mix.

Show answer

B. Without it, a small test set might get almost none of the rare cases.

4A column size holds "small", "medium", or "large". Is one-hot encoding the only sensible choice?

  • One-hot is the safe default for categories with no order, but these have one.

  • For ordered categories, the numbers' order means something real. For unordered ones like stations, it doesn't.

  • Most scikit-learn models need numbers, so text has to be encoded first.

Show answer

B. For ordered categories, the numbers' order means something real. For unordered ones like stations, it doesn't.

Key takeaways

  • Split before anything else, and judge the model on the test rows, once, at the end.
  • train_test_split returns training features, test features, training targets, test targets, in that order. Add stratify=y for classification.
  • k-NN measures distance, so features with big numbers drown out the rest. StandardScaler gives every feature mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
  • Preprocessing steps learn from training rows only: fit on train, transform on both. A pipeline enforces this for you.
  • One-hot encoding turns a category into 0-or-1 columns; OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore") copes with categories it hasn't seen.

What you'll learn

  • Split a classification dataset with stratify and check that both parts keep the same class mix.
  • Measure a do-nothing baseline before trusting any model's accuracy.
  • Scale numeric columns and one-hot encode a text column, fitting each step on training rows only.

A small studio has launched a puzzle game. After each new player's first day, the studio wants to guess whether that player will still be playing a week later, so it can send a well-timed tip to the ones likely to drift away. You have day-one data for 400 past players and whether each came back on day 7.

The model is k-nearest neighbors, unchanged from start to finish. Only the data preparation changes, and here's the plan:

Start a notebook called m3-player-prep.ipynb.

#Step 1: Make the player table

As in Module 2, the data comes from a seeded random generator so your numbers match this page. In real life this would be an export from the game's analytics.

Look at the min and max rows. Sessions run from 1 to 12 and levels from 1 to 36, but coins run into the thousands. device is text. And only 37% of players came back, so the classes aren't balanced. Each of those three facts shapes one step below.

#Step 2: Split first, with stratify

The split happens before anything learns from the data:

Both parts have the same share of returning players, thanks to stratify=y. From here on, X_test and y_test are only touched to score.

#Step 3: Measure the bar to clear

If you guessed "won't come back" for every player, how often would you be right?

About 63%, with zero intelligence involved. With unbalanced classes, an accuracy that sounds decent can be worse than this lazy guess, so this is the number every model has to beat.

#Step 4: k-NN on the raw numbers

Try the model on the three numeric columns exactly as they are:

Worse than always guessing "not back". The reason is the coin count. Two players who differ by 3,000 coins are "far apart", even if their sessions and levels are identical, and a gap of 10 sessions barely registers. So each player's five nearest neighbors are simply the players with similar coin counts, and in this game coins say nothing about who returns.

#Step 5: Scale the numbers

Fit a StandardScaler on the training rows, then transform both sets with what it learned:

mean_ and scale_ are the averages and standard deviations the scaler learned from the 300 training players. Each column is now measured in "standard deviations from the training average", so a big gap in sessions counts as much as a big gap in coins. Accuracy jumps well past the baseline.

#Step 6: One-hot encode the device

The device column is still unused, and web players behave quite differently. Encode it, fitting on training rows only:

np.hstack glues the three scaled number columns and the three device columns side by side into one six-column table. Two web players are now "nearer" each other than a web player and an iOS player, which is exactly the information the model was missing.

#Step 7: Put it all in one pipeline

Steps 5 and 6 work, but there are six separate fit and transform calls to keep straight, and one slip (like fitting the encoder on X_test) would leak. make_column_transformer says which preprocessing goes with which columns, and make_pipeline puts the model after it:

Same accuracy as Step 6, from one fit call on the raw training table. The pipeline fits the scaler and encoder on whatever you pass to fit (the training rows) and only transforms whatever you pass to score or predict.

What you'll learn

  • Reproduce StandardScaler by hand to understand exactly what it learns.

#Warm-up: an 80/20 split

Split the iris data so 20% is held out for testing, with random_state=7, and print the shapes of all four pieces.

120 rows to learn from, 30 to test on, and the first numbers of X and y agree within each part.

#Exercise 1: The sorted-data trap

Someone made a test set by taking the last 30 rows of iris. Count how many flowers of each species end up in their training and test sets. Then do the same for a stratified train_test_split with test_size=30 and random_state=7.

Need a hint?

np.bincount(labels) counts how many 0s, 1s, and 2s are in an array. Slicing with y_iris[:120] and y_iris[120:] gives the sliced version.

Show solution

The sliced test set contains only virginica, so its score would say nothing about setosa or versicolor, and the model trained on just 20 virginica. The stratified split puts exactly a fifth of each species in the test set. minlength=3 makes bincount print a 0 for missing species instead of a shorter array.

#Exercise 2: How much does stratify matter?

Using the breast cancer data, split with test_size=0.2 and random_state=3, once without stratify and once with stratify=y. For each, print the share of malignant samples (target 0) in the full data, the training set, and the test set.

Need a hint?

(y == 0).mean() gives the fraction of rows where the target is 0, because True counts as 1 and False as 0. Loop over [None, y] as the value of stratify to avoid writing the split twice.

Show solution

Without stratifying, this split happens to put fewer malignant samples in the test set (35.1% versus 37.3% overall). That looks small, but with 114 test rows it's about two fewer of the cases you most need to catch. Stratified, the test share is as close to the true share as whole rows allow.

#Exercise 3: StandardScaler by hand

Split the breast cancer data with random_state=0 and stratify=y. Compute each feature's mean and standard deviation from the training rows with NumPy, standardize the test rows by hand, and check that your result matches StandardScaler().fit(X_train).transform(X_test).

Need a hint?

X_train.mean(axis=0) gives one mean per column (axis=0 means "down the rows"). Use X_train.std(axis=0) for the spread. Watch out if you try pandas: its .std() divides by n − 1 by default, while StandardScaler divides by n, so they differ slightly. np.allclose(a, b) checks whether two arrays match up to rounding.

Show solution

StandardScaler is these three lines with some safety checks. It remembers means and stds (as mean_ and scale_) from training, and every later transform uses those same numbers. The test rows are measured against the training average, which is what keeps them honest.

#Exercise 4: Fix the leaky code

This code runs and prints a good score, but it breaks two rules from the Notes lesson. Find both, then rewrite it as a pipeline that's fitted on training rows only.

Need a hint?

Look for every call to fit or fit_transform and ask which rows it learned from. One happens before the split. Another learns a second, different set of means from the test rows.

Show solution

Bug 1: the scaler is fitted on all of X before splitting, so test rows shape the training data's scaling. Bug 2: the test set is scaled again with fit_transform, using its own mean and standard deviation, so it's measured with a different ruler from the training set.

The honest score is exactly the same as the leaky one here, and that's what makes this bug so easy to ship: nothing looks wrong. With 569 rows, the means and standard deviations hardly change whichever rows they're learned from, so the damage is invisible. With a small dataset, or steps that learn more (like picking features), it can be large. The pipeline makes both bugs impossible to write.

#Exercise 5: A category the encoder never saw

An encoder is trained on players from Android and iOS. Then a web player shows up. Run this, read the error, and fix the encoder so the web player gets all-zero device columns.

Need a hint?

The last line of the error names the unknown category. OneHotEncoder has a setting that decides what to do in that situation; its default is to raise an error.

Show solution

With handle_unknown="ignore", a new category becomes a row of zeros: "none of the devices I know". For a model running in an app, that's usually better than crashing. If a new category turns up often, it's a sign to retrain with data that includes it.

#Exercise 6: Does scaling always help?

The digits dataset has 64 pixel features, each already measured on the same 0 to 16 brightness scale. Predict first: will StandardScaler help k-NN here? Then measure it with a stratified split (random_state=0), comparing k-NN with and without the scaler.

Need a hint?

Build two models: KNeighborsClassifier() and make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier()). Fit both on the same training rows and compare score on the same test rows.

Show solution

Scaling made it slightly worse. The pixels already share one unit, so there's no imbalance to fix. Worse, pixels near the edge of the image are almost always 0 and only occasionally faint. Standardizing divides by their tiny standard deviation, which blows that occasional faint smudge up into a big number, so noise at the edges starts to matter as much as the strokes in the middle. Scaling fixes mismatched units; it isn't a free upgrade.

A resale website wants to flag listings likely to sell within a week. Each listing has a price, the bike's age, its kind (road, mountain, kids), and the city. Build the data with the cell below, then:

Kids' bikes sell fast, and so do mountain bikes in Denver. Neither fact is visible in price and age alone, so the numbers-only model is only a little better than the baseline. m4-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Classify a new point by hand with k-nearest neighbors, then check the answer with scikit-learn.
  • Explain how small and large values of k change the decision boundary and the test score.
  • Fit a linear regression, read its slope and intercept, and compute residuals and mean squared error.
  • Describe gradient descent as "step downhill on the loss" and follow one update by hand.
  • Choose between k-NN and a line for a given problem.

A friend moves to your city and asks which pizza place they'll like. You could study cheese chemistry, or you could think of the three people you know whose taste is most like your friend's and recommend whatever most of them like. That second plan is k-nearest neighbors, and you already used it in Module 1 without opening it up.

Now your friend asks how long their bike commute will be. Nearby examples would work here too, but there's another way: draw the straight line that best fits past trips (distance against minutes) and read the answer off the line. That's linear regression. This lesson takes both ideas apart.

#k-NN: let the closest examples vote

To predict for a new example, k-nearest neighbors does three things:

  1. Measure the distance from the new example to every training example.
  2. Keep the k closest.
  3. For classification, take a majority vote of their labels. For regression, average their values.

That's the whole algorithm. Calling fit just stores the training data (organized for fast searching); the real work happens at predict time. "Distance" is ordinary straight-line distance: for two features, it's Pythagoras, the square root of (difference in x)² + (difference in y)².

Here are eight labeled points and one new one. Compute every distance, keep the three smallest, and vote:

np.argsort returns the positions of the distances from smallest to largest, so [:3] picks the three nearest. One is red and two are blue, so blue wins. Notice the two closest points are tied at 1.41, one of each color: with k = 2 the vote would be a tie, which is why odd values of k are popular.

scikit-learn reaches the same answer, and its kneighbors method shows you which neighbors it used:

The same three positions, the same distances. (Ties between equal distances can be broken differently, so on other data the order may vary.)

#How k changes the boundary

The decision boundary is the line where the model's answer flips from one class to the other. To see it, color every spot on a grid by what the model would predict there. Here are 300 points in two interleaved crescents, with some noise, and three choices of k:

Read the printout next to the pictures:

  • k = 1 has 100% training accuracy, as you saw in Module 3: every point is its own nearest neighbor. The boundary wraps around individual noisy points, making little islands that won't hold up on new data.
  • k = 15 draws a smooth S-curve that follows the real crescents. It makes some training mistakes on purpose, and it scores best on the test set.
  • k = 100 averages over nearly half of the 225 training points for every prediction, so the boundary is too stiff to follow the curve, and both scores drop.

Small k is too sensitive to noise; large k is too blunt. The best k lies somewhere in between, and the only way to find it is to try several and compare them on data the model didn't train on (you'll do that in the practice).

#Predicting numbers with a line

k-NN can predict numbers too (KNeighborsRegressor averages the neighbors' values). But when the target rises or falls steadily with a feature, a straight line describes that more simply. Take the diabetes data again, this time with the real, unscaled body mass index:

A line has two numbers. The slope (coef_) says how much the prediction rises for each extra unit of the feature: about 10 progression points per BMI point. The intercept (intercept_) is where the line would cross zero BMI, which no living person has, so read it as "the number that puts the line in the right place", not as a fact about patients.

#Residuals: how wrong the line is, point by point

For each patient, the residual is the actual value minus the line's prediction. Positive means the line guessed too low; negative means too high. Here they are as vertical gaps, drawn for 60 patients so the picture stays readable:

To score the whole line with one number, square every residual and average them. That's the mean squared error (MSE), the line's loss:

Squaring does two jobs: it makes every miss count as positive (so misses above and below don't cancel out), and it punishes one big miss more than several small ones. "Fitting a line" means finding the slope and intercept with the smallest possible MSE. No other line through this data has a lower one.

#How a model finds the best line: gradient descent

LinearRegression finds the best line with an exact formula. Most models, including the neural networks behind image and language tools, have no such formula. They learn with gradient descent, and a line is the clearest place to see how it works.

Here's the intuition. Picture the loss as a hilly landscape, where every spot is one possible line and the height is its MSE. You're standing somewhere in fog and want to reach the bottom. You can't see the valley, but you can feel which way the ground slopes under your feet. So you take a step downhill, feel again, and repeat. Steep ground means you're far from the bottom, so take a big step; flat ground means you're close.

Let's make that precise for a line through the origin, prediction = w * x, on three points that lie exactly on y = 2x. The slope of the loss with respect to w (its gradient) is the average of 2 * (w * x - y) * x. The update rule is: new w = old w − learning rate × gradient. Step through five updates and watch w creep toward 2:

The first gradient is large and negative (the line is far too flat), so w jumps from 0 to 0.933. Each later gradient is smaller, because the line is getting closer, so the steps shrink: 1.431, 1.697, 1.838, 1.914. The learning rate sets the step size. Too small and it takes forever; too big and you leap over the valley.

The same loop with two numbers to learn (slope and intercept) fits the BMI line. Here's its loss after every step, next to the line at a few moments along the way. BMI is standardized first, because gradient descent, like k-NN, works much better when features are on a similar scale:

Step 0 is a flat line at zero, with a huge loss. Within a few steps the line has jumped up to the middle of the data and tilted, and by step 40 it has settled where the loss can't go much lower. You'll write this loop yourself in the next lesson and check it against LinearRegression.

#Which one when?

k-nearest neighbors Linear regression
Predicts categories (KNeighborsClassifier) or numbers (KNeighborsRegressor) numbers
What fit does stores the training rows finds the best slope(s) and intercept
Needs scaled features yes, distances depend on units not for LinearRegression; yes for gradient descent
Handles curved patterns yes, it follows the data locally no, it's one straight line (or flat surface)
Predicts outside the training range no, it can only repeat values it has seen yes, the line keeps going, for better or worse
Easy to explain "these 5 similar cases said so" "each extra unit adds this much"

⚠️ Watch out

Using a classifier for a number. KNeighborsClassifier treats every distinct target value as its own category. Give it a target with decimals, like these progression scores shifted by 0.5, and scikit-learn refuses:

"Continuous" is scikit-learn's word for a target of decimal numbers. Use KNeighborsRegressor or LinearRegression for those. (With whole numbers, it won't even raise an error; it will quietly treat 151 and 152 as unrelated classes, so pick the model by what the target means.)

Trusting a line far from the data. The BMI line keeps rising forever, and at a BMI of 10 it predicts a negative progression score. A line is only trustworthy across the range of data it was fitted on.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1k-NN with k = 1 gets 100% training accuracy and 85% test accuracy. With k = 9 it gets 92% and 91%. What's going on?

  • Training accuracy for k = 1 is always perfect, because each point is its own neighbor. The test score is what counts.

  • Averaging over more neighbors stops single odd points from deciding the answer.

  • A 6-point gap together with a jagged-versus-smooth boundary is a pattern, not luck.

Show answer

B. Averaging over more neighbors stops single odd points from deciding the answer.

2A line is price = 3.2 * size + 50. One house has size 100 and sold for 400. What's its residual?

  • That's 3.2 × 100 + 50, which is the prediction, not the residual.

  • The residual is actual minus predicted: 400 − 370 = 30. The line guessed $30 too low.

  • That would be predicted minus actual. The usual definition is actual minus predicted.

Show answer

B. The residual is actual minus predicted: 400 − 370 = 30. The line guessed $30 too low.

3In gradient descent, the gradient for w comes out as a large positive number. What does the update do?

  • The update subtracts learning rate × gradient, so a big positive gradient means a big step down.

  • A positive gradient means the loss rises as w rises, so downhill is toward smaller w.

  • A large gradient means steep ground, which means you're far from the bottom.

Show answer

A. The update subtracts learning rate × gradient, so a big positive gradient means a big step down.

4You want to predict a house's price from its size, and some new houses are bigger than any in your data. Which model is the safer start?

  • For a house bigger than all the training houses, k-NN can only average the biggest ones it has seen, so it can't predict a higher price.

  • Extending a line a little past the data is reasonable. Extending it very far is risky for any model.

  • Size is one of the strongest predictors of price.

Show answer

B. Extending a line a little past the data is reasonable. Extending it very far is risky for any model.

Key takeaways

  • k-NN stores the training rows and, for each new row, lets the k nearest ones vote (classification) or averages them (regression).
  • Small k makes a jagged boundary that fits noise; large k makes a blunt one. Pick k by comparing scores on unseen data.
  • Linear regression predicts slope × feature + intercept, choosing the slope and intercept that make the mean squared error smallest.
  • A residual is actual minus predicted; MSE averages the squared residuals.
  • Gradient descent repeatedly steps against the gradient of the loss. The learning rate sets the step size.

#Further reading

  • Nearest neighbors (opens in a new tab): scikit-learn's user guide, including distance-weighted voting with weights="distance".
  • Gradient descent (opens in a new tab), from Google's Machine Learning Crash Course: the loss landscape and convergence, with diagrams.
  • Linear models (opens in a new tab): the math behind LinearRegression and its many relatives.

What you'll learn

  • Write functions for a line's predictions, its mean squared error, and its gradients.
  • Turn those into a working gradient descent loop and plot its loss falling.
  • Check a from-scratch model against scikit-learn's LinearRegression, including converting back to original units.
  • Compare a line and k-NN regression on one feature and on all ten, using test-set error.

You'll build a model-fitting algorithm from nothing but NumPy: about fifteen lines that find the best straight line through the diabetes data by walking downhill on the loss. Then you'll put it up against scikit-learn. Here's the comparison your notebook will print at the end:

MAE is the mean absolute error from Module 2, in progression points. Lower is better. Open m4-gradient-descent.ipynb and start building.

#Step 1: Load the data and standardize BMI

Use the unscaled diabetes data so BMI has its real values. Then standardize it, because gradient descent takes far more steps when a feature's numbers are large (you'll see why in the practice).

Keep bmi_mean and bmi_std. You'll need them in Step 5 to turn your answer back into real BMI units.

#Step 2: Write the line and its loss

Two small functions: one makes predictions for a slope w and intercept b, the other scores them with mean squared error. Try three guesses by hand:

Each guess is better than the last: putting the line at the right height (b = 150) cuts the loss by more than half, and tilting it upward (w = 40) cuts it again. Guess-and-check works, but it's slow, and you'd never know when to stop. Gradient descent tells you which way to adjust, and by how much.

#Step 3: Compute the gradients

The gradient says how fast the loss changes as you nudge each number. For mean squared error on a line, calculus gives two short formulas. Let error = prediction - y:

  • gradient for w: the average of 2 * error * x
  • gradient for b: the average of 2 * error

You don't need the calculus to use them. Read them as: "if the line is too high where x is large, lower the slope; if it's too high on average, lower the intercept."

Both gradients are negative, meaning "the loss goes down if you increase these", so the step increases both. One step took the loss from about 29,000 to about 20,000.

#Step 4: Loop it

Repeat that step and record the loss each time:

Each step reduces the error between prediction and truth a little, and the gradients shrink as the line gets closer, so the curve flattens out on its own. After 60 steps the changes are too small to matter.

#Step 5: Check your answer against scikit-learn

If your code is right, LinearRegression should find the same line. Fit it on the same standardized x:

They agree to three decimal places. x.reshape(-1, 1) turns the flat array into a one-column table, the shape fit needs (the same fix as the Series bug in Module 2).

Your slope is in "progression points per standard deviation of BMI", which nobody thinks in. Convert it back to real BMI units. Since x = (bmi - mean) / std, the line w * x + b equals (w / std) * bmi + (b - w * mean / std):

The same line as the Notes lesson: about 10.2 progression points per BMI point. You've reproduced scikit-learn's answer with an algorithm you wrote yourself.

#Step 6: Race the line against k-NN on BMI alone

k-NN regression predicts a patient's score by averaging the scores of the k patients with the closest BMI. Draw each model's predictions across a range of BMIs, including some beyond the data (the dashed lines mark the smallest and largest BMI in the dataset):

With k = 5, k-NN chases small clusters of patients and wobbles. With k = 40 it's smoother and looks a lot like the line, with a slight curve. Past the dashed lines, k-NN can only repeat the average of the most extreme patients it knows, so it goes flat, while the line keeps rising. The k = 40 curve flattens even before the right-hand line, because above a BMI of about 37 the same 40 patients are always the nearest. Whether that's good depends on whether the trend really continues.

#Step 7: Race them on all ten features

One feature only tells part of the story. Use all ten, split off a test set, and compare test MAE. k-NN gets a scaler in a pipeline, as Module 3 taught; the line doesn't need one:

Every model beats the baseline by a wide margin, and the line wins narrowly. With 442 patients and a mostly steady relationship between the measurements and the outcome, a straight-line rule is hard to beat. k-NN would shine on a pattern with bends that a line can't follow, like the crescents in the Notes lesson. Neither model is "better" in general; the data decides.

#The finished line-fitter

Your from-scratch gradient descent, in one cell, with a check against scikit-learn built in:

Check your understanding

3 questions

1In Step 3, both gradients at (0, 0) were negative. Why did the update increase w and b?

  • The learning rate was 0.1, a positive number.

  • A negative gradient means the loss falls as the value rises, so the downhill step raises it.

  • The direction depends entirely on the gradient's sign. Start above the best line and the first steps go down.

Show answer

B. A negative gradient means the loss falls as the value rises, so the downhill step raises it.

2Why did the build standardize BMI before running gradient descent?

  • Standardizing changes the units, not the line. Step 5's conversion recovered the same slope as scikit-learn on raw BMI.

  • It accepts any scale. That's why the raw-BMI check in Step 5 worked.

  • The best possible line makes the same predictions in either unit, so its MSE is the same.

Show answer

A. Standardizing changes the units, not the line. Step 5's conversion recovered the same slope as scikit-learn on raw BMI.

3For a patient with BMI 48, above everyone in the data, what does the k = 40 k-NN model predict?

  • That's what the line does. k-NN can only average scores it has already seen.

  • Every BMI above the maximum has the same 40 nearest neighbors, so the prediction stays flat.

  • k-NN will predict for any input; it just can't extrapolate.

Show answer

B. Every BMI above the maximum has the same 40 nearest neighbors, so the prediction stays flat.

Key takeaways

  • Gradient descent needs three pieces: a prediction function, a loss, and the loss's gradients. The loop repeatedly steps each parameter against its gradient.
  • A from-scratch model is worth checking against a trusted library. Matching answers mean both your math and your code are right.
  • Standardizing a feature changes the units of the slope, not the line itself; you can convert back.
  • k-NN regression follows local wiggles and goes flat outside the data; a line follows one steady trend and extends it.
  • On the full diabetes data, a line narrowly beats k-NN on test error. On curved data, it often goes the other way.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Rerun fit_line with learning_rate=0.01 and learning_rate=0.9. Plot all the histories on one chart. The practice lesson digs into what you'll see.
  • Extend fit_line to two features, bmi and bp (blood pressure): one more weight, one more gradient line, the same loop. Compare its weights with LinearRegression on both columns.
  • Try KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=20, weights="distance"), which gives closer neighbors a bigger say, and see whether its test MAE improves.
