What you'll learn

  • Explain each requirement of the capstone brief and why it's there.
  • Choose a project that fits your level, and say what makes it hard.
  • Write a data card that describes your dataset honestly.
  • Fill in a plan that fixes your metric, baseline, models, and split before you train anything.

Suppose your school's robotics club wants software that reads handwritten scores off judges' sheets, and someone asks you which model to use. "k-NN, it got 98%" is an answer. It isn't a recommendation. A recommendation says 98% of what, measured how, compared with which alternatives, and what goes wrong in the other 2%.

The capstone asks you to produce exactly that: a comparison of classical models on one dataset that a skeptical reader can check and can't easily poke holes in. Everything you need, you've already practiced in Modules 2 to 7. This module puts it in one notebook.

#The brief

Build one Colab notebook that compares at least three models on one dataset and ends with a recommendation. It must include:

  1. A documented dataset. One that ships with scikit-learn, one you generate in the notebook, or a small CSV you're allowed to use, with a data card (below).
  2. A protected test set. Split it off first, and score it once, at the end.
  3. Preprocessing inside pipelines, so no fold or test row ever leaks into a scaler or encoder.
  4. A baseline (DummyClassifier or DummyRegressor) and at least three real models from the ones you've learned: k-NN, linear or logistic regression, and decision trees. Two versions of one model type with meaningfully different settings can count as two.
  5. A cross-validated comparison on the same folds, with at least two metrics chosen before you look at results.
  6. A fit diagnosis: at least one training-versus-validation curve, and a paragraph on where your models underfit or overfit.
  7. Error analysis: look at the specific examples your final model gets wrong and describe any pattern.
  8. A recommendation of one model, with the evidence for it, its limits, and what you'd try next.

Each requirement blocks one way of fooling yourself. The test set stops you from grading your own homework. Pipelines stop leaks. The baseline stops you from celebrating 90% accuracy on a dataset that's 90% one class. Cross-validation stops one lucky split from picking the winner. Error analysis stops a single number from hiding what the model can't do.

#Pick a project

Project Dataset Task What makes it interesting
Iris species (starter) load_iris 3-class classification Every model scores above 90%, so the challenge is arguing honestly when results are tied.
Handwritten digits (middle) load_digits 10-class classification A 10×10 confusion matrix and real images of the digits each model misreads. Lesson 2 builds this one as the worked example.
Signal hidden in noise (middle) make_friedman1 Regression Only 5 of the 10 features matter, and you know the true formula. Can any model find the useful ones?
Rare-event detector (harder) make_classification with weights=[0.97], or your own simulation like the icy roads Imbalanced classification Accuracy is useless, so you'll need precision and recall, a threshold chosen on validation data, and a story for what each mistake costs.
Your own small CSV (stretch) A file you upload to Colab Your choice Real, messy data, but you must document where it came from and that you're allowed to use it. No personal information about real people.

If you can't decide, take the digits. The worked example in the next lesson gives you a path to follow, and you can make it your own in the error analysis.

Here's a first look at four of the options. Run it and notice the class balance in each:

The rare-event set has about 70 positives in 2,000 rows. A model that never predicts the positive class scores above 96% accuracy there, which is exactly why that project needs different metrics.

#Write a data card first

A data card is a short description of a dataset that someone else could use to decide whether to trust your results. Write it in a Colab text cell at the top of your notebook, before any modeling code. Fill in every line, even when the answer is "unknown".

That last line matters even for toy data. "A misread 7 changes a judge's score" makes you think about which errors to analyze, and it will shape your recommendation.

#Make the plan before you train anything

The fastest way to fool yourself is to try things until a number looks good and then decide that number is the one that matters. Writing the plan first takes away that temptation. Copy this into a second text cell:

The last line is the most useful one. Deciding in advance how you'll break a near-tie means the results can't talk you into whatever you hoped for.

#The milestones

Lesson 2 walks through each milestone with code. Lesson 3 covers checking your notebook, presenting it, and the full rubric. A quick preview of how it's graded: correctness of the process (no leaks, test set used once) counts as much as the quality of your models, and a clear, honest recommendation counts more than a high score.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1Halfway through, you notice the test-set accuracy of your tree is higher than its cross-validation score, so you switch your recommendation to the tree. What's wrong?

  • It's realistic only until you use it to make a choice. After that, it's just another validation score.

  • The plan says the test set is scored once, after the decision. Choose with cross-validation, then confirm.

  • Trees are fine. The problem is how the choice was made.

Show answer

B. The plan says the test set is scored once, after the decision. Choose with cross-validation, then confirm.

2For the rare-event project, which plan line most needs changing from the digits plan?

  • Five folds work for both, as long as they're stratified.

  • With 3% positives, accuracy rewards a model that never finds a single positive.

  • The baseline matters even more here, because it shows how high accuracy can be with zero skill.

Show answer

B. With 3% positives, accuracy rewards a model that never finds a single positive.

Key takeaways

  • The brief's eight requirements each block a specific way of fooling yourself.
  • Pick a project by what makes it interesting, not by which one will get the highest score.
  • A data card and a written plan come before any modeling code.
  • Decide in advance how you'll break near-ties, so results can't change your rules.

#Further reading

  • scikit-learn: toy datasets (opens in a new tab): the official descriptions of iris, digits, and the other built-in sets, which make a good starting point for your data card.
  • scikit-learn: choosing the right estimator (opens in a new tab): a flowchart for picking candidate models by task and data size.

What you'll learn

  • Get a minimal notebook running end to end before adding anything else.
  • Compare a baseline and four models on the same folds with two metrics.
  • Diagnose fit with a cross-validated depth curve and a k sweep.
  • Score the chosen model once on the test set and analyze the specific mistakes.
  • Write a recommendation backed by your numbers.

This lesson builds the digits project from Lesson 1 as a worked example. If you chose a different project, follow the same milestones with your own data; the table near the end lists what to swap. Each milestone ends with a notebook that runs from top to bottom, so if you run out of time, you still have something complete to hand in.

#The starter notebook

Get this running first, with your own dataset swapped in if you're not doing digits. A tiny notebook that runs end to end beats a fancy one that crashes halfway.

Two lines of output, and the skeleton of the whole project is already there: a locked test set, shared folds, a baseline, and a model that beats it. Every milestone below grows one part of this.

#Milestone 1: Data card and a look at the data

Fill in the data card from Lesson 1 in a text cell. For digits it reads:

Then look at real examples, because a data card written without looking at the data is a guess:

At 8×8 pixels, some digits are hard even for people. That's worth one sentence in your write-up, because it sets expectations for the error analysis.

#Milestone 2: An evaluation helper and the baseline

Your plan named two metrics. For ten balanced classes, accuracy is reasonable, and macro F1 (F1 computed for each digit, then averaged so every digit counts equally) catches a model that's great at most digits but bad at one. Write one helper so every model is measured identically:

The baseline guesses the most common digit every time and is right about 10% of the time, which is chance with ten classes. Its macro F1 is near 0 because it never predicts nine of the ten digits.

#Milestone 3: Four models on the same folds

max_iter=1000 gives logistic regression enough steps to finish fitting 64 features; with the default, Colab may show a ConvergenceWarning.

Two findings here are worth writing up. First, the tree's training accuracy is far above its CV accuracy, a gap you'll investigate next. Second, scaling made k-NN worse. That's the opposite of what you might expect from Module 3. All 64 pixels already share one unit (ink, 0 to 16). StandardScaler stretches every pixel to the same spread, so a corner pixel that's almost always blank gets as much say in the distance as a pixel in the middle of the digit. Scaling fixes features measured in different units; here it amplifies noise. That's the kind of observation that makes a capstone more than a table of numbers.

#Milestone 4: Diagnose fit

Draw a cross-validated curve for the model with the biggest train/CV gap, the tree:

Past depth 10, the tree memorizes the training digits (training accuracy reaches 1.0) while its CV accuracy stalls around 0.85. No depth makes it competitive: asking about one pixel at a time is a poor way to read handwriting. That's a model limitation, not a tuning problem, and saying so is a legitimate finding.

Now tune k for the winning family, raw-pixel k-NN:

k=1 has the best CV mean, but k=3 is within its standard deviation and is steadier from fold to fold. The plan said near-ties go to the less extreme setting, and k=1 is the most extreme a k-NN can be (one mislabeled training digit fools it every time). So the choice is k=3, decided by a rule written before the results came in.

#Milestone 5: Choose, then test once

The test accuracy lands right next to the cross-validated estimate, so the process held up. This is the only time the test set is used.

#Milestone 6: Look at every mistake

With five errors, you can look at each one. (With fifty, you'd look at the most common confusions from the matrix instead.)

Look for a pattern before writing anything. Here, four of the five mistakes involve an 8 or a 9, and three involve a 3 (either as the truth or the guess). In an 8×8 grid, the loops of an 8 or 9 and the curves of a 3 differ by only a few pixels. Your write-up should say which mistakes happen and suggest why; "the model is 98.6% accurate" says neither.

#Milestone 7: Write the recommendation

Use this shape in a text cell, and fill in every bracket with a number from your notebook:

For the digits example:

Use k-NN with k=3 on raw pixels. In 5-fold cross-validation on 1,437 training digits it scored 0.985 ± 0.003 accuracy, ahead of logistic regression and scaled k-NN at about 0.97, and far ahead of the 0.10 baseline. On the untouched test set it scored 0.986. A decision tree topped out near 0.85 at any depth while memorizing its training data. k=1 scored about the same as k=3 but is more fragile, so we chose k=3 by a rule set before testing. Limits: most of its five test errors involve 3, 8, and 9, and with only 8×8 images and a few dozen writers, it may do worse on new handwriting styles. Next step: collect a few digits from new writers and check whether accuracy holds.

#Adapting the milestones to your project

If your project is... Change this
Regression (make_friedman1 or a numeric CSV) KFold instead of StratifiedKFold; DummyRegressor; regressors instead of classifiers; scoring ["neg_mean_absolute_error", "r2"] (flip the sign of MAE); error analysis looks at the largest misses.
Rare events Scoring ["recall", "precision"] or "f1"; choose a threshold on a validation split as in Module 6; error analysis looks at the missed positives.
Iris Everything ties, so Milestone 7's "why not the others" needs care: use the std and your plan's tie-break rule.
Your own CSV Add encoding for text columns inside the pipeline (Module 3), and check for columns that leak the answer before Milestone 1.

Key takeaways

  • A minimal end-to-end notebook comes first; each milestone grows it without breaking it.
  • One evaluate helper and one folds object make every comparison identical.
  • Fit diagnosis can show that a model is limited, not just badly tuned; both are findings.
  • Near-ties are settled by a rule written in the plan, not by which number you like.
  • Error analysis means looking at the actual mistakes and naming a pattern.

What you'll learn

  • Write a cell of automatic checks that catch the most common capstone mistakes.
  • Prove the notebook reruns cleanly from a fresh session.
  • Make a results chart whose title states the finding.
  • Present the comparison in about three minutes, limits included.
  • Score your own work with the rubric before anyone else does.

The night before a presentation is the worst time to discover that your notebook only worked because of a cell you deleted on Tuesday. This lesson is about catching problems while they're cheap: with code that checks your process, a clean rerun, and a self-review against the rubric your work will be graded on.

#Write checks, not hopes

A model comparison can be wrong in ways no error message will ever reveal. A test row sneaks into training; a scaler sits outside its pipeline; a rerun gives different numbers. Each of those can be turned into a line of code that prints PASS or FAIL. Here's a checks cell, shown on a small iris comparison so it runs quickly. Copy the check lines into your own notebook, after Milestone 3, and change the names to match yours.

Each check matches a rule from the brief. The row-number trick deserves a note: passing rows as an extra array to train_test_split splits it exactly like X and y, so you can prove which original rows ended up where. The reproducibility check only passes if every random step has a random_state; remove the one in StratifiedKFold and it will fail on most runs.

🧪 Try it yourself

Break something on purpose to see a check catch it. Replace make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier()) with plain KNeighborsClassifier() but keep the name "k-NN (scaled)", as if you'd forgotten the scaler. Rerun and watch the pipeline check fail. Then put the pipeline back.

#Rerun from a fresh session

Checks only help if the notebook runs at all. Choose Runtime → Restart session and run all. Colab wipes every variable and runs each cell once, top to bottom. If it reaches the end with no errors and the same numbers as before, the notebook is reproducible. If a cell fails, it depended on something you ran by hand and later changed or deleted; fix it now.

Then check the numbers themselves. Do the CV scores in your write-up match what's printed? Every number in your recommendation should be copied from output, not remembered.

#Polish the notebook

Someone reading your notebook should be able to follow it without you in the room. Before you hand it in:

  • The data card and plan are text cells at the very top.
  • Each milestone starts with a short text cell saying what it does and what you found.
  • Every chart has a title, labeled axes, and units where they apply.
  • Printed numbers are rounded to 3 decimal places, not 16.
  • Dead experiments are deleted, not commented out. (Keep them in a separate scratch notebook if you like them.)
  • Every random_state is set, so your numbers are the reader's numbers.

The single biggest upgrade is a results chart whose title is the conclusion, not the topic. "Model accuracy" makes the reader work it out; "k-NN on raw pixels reads digits best" tells them. Here's the digits comparison from Lesson 2, polished:

Sorted bars, one highlight color for the recommendation, gray for the baseline, and numbers printed on the bars so nobody has to squint at the axis. The error bars stay, because they show which gaps are real.

#Present it in three minutes

You won't have time to show the whole notebook, and you shouldn't. Lead with the answer, then earn it:

  1. The question and the answer (20 seconds). "We wanted a model to read handwritten digits. We recommend k-NN with k=3, which read 98.6% of test digits correctly."
  2. The data (20 seconds). One sentence from your data card and one picture of the data.
  3. The contest (40 seconds). The polished chart. Say how the comparison was kept fair: same folds, pipelines, a locked test set.
  4. The diagnosis (30 seconds). One fit curve and what it showed, such as the tree memorizing at every depth past 10.
  5. The mistakes (40 seconds). The error gallery and the pattern you found.
  6. Limits and next step (30 seconds). What the model can't be trusted with, and one experiment you'd run next.

Say the limits yourself, before someone in the audience does. "It might struggle with handwriting styles it hasn't seen" sounds like expertise. Being asked about it and having no answer sounds like you didn't look.

#The rubric

Grade yourself honestly before you submit. Each row is scored 1 to 4.

Criterion 4: Excellent 3: Solid 2: Developing 1: Missing
Data and plan Complete data card and plan, written before modeling, with a tie-break rule Data card and plan present, a field or two thin Partial data card or plan written after results Neither
Leak-free process Test set split first and used once; all preprocessing in pipelines; checks cell passes Test set used once; one small preprocessing slip Test set used more than once, or scaler outside pipeline No held-out test set
Fair comparison Baseline plus 3+ models, same folds, 2+ metrics with mean ± std Baseline plus 3 models, same folds, one metric Fewer than 3 models, or different splits per model Single model
Fit diagnosis Training-vs-validation curve with a clear explanation of under- or overfitting Curve present, explanation brief Train and validation numbers mentioned, no curve Not addressed
Error analysis Specific mistakes examined, a pattern named, and a likely reason given Mistakes listed with some pattern Confusion matrix shown without comment Not addressed
Recommendation One model chosen with evidence, honest limits, and a concrete next step Clear choice with evidence; limits thin Choice stated with little evidence No recommendation
Notebook quality Restart-and-run-all works; text cells guide the reader; charts titled with findings Runs cleanly; some sections unexplained Runs only with manual fixes Doesn't run

A 4 in every row doesn't require a high accuracy. An iris project with a careful tie-break argument can outscore a digits project with a leaky pipeline.

#Reflect, then keep going

Answer these in a final text cell. They're for you, but they're also what an interviewer or teacher will ask:

  • Which result surprised you, and what did you learn from it?
  • If you had to defend your recommendation against the runner-up, what's your strongest piece of evidence?
  • What's one thing about your process you'd do differently next time?

Where to go from here: decision trees grow up into random forests and gradient boosting, which combine hundreds of trees and are among the strongest models for tables of data. The loops you wrote by hand to tune settings become GridSearchCV. Threshold choices become ROC and precision-recall curves. You already understand the ideas underneath each of these, which is the hard part.
